paragraphs.title: The Psalm’s Heading and the Fool

easy.explanation: The heading identifies it as a maskil of David.
easy.q: To whom is the psalm attributed in its heading?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.”
easy.q: What does the fool say in his heart?

answers: He becomes corrupt and acts wickedly
easy.explanation: The passage says that they are corrupt and have done abominable iniquity.
easy.q: How does the fool act according to the passage?

answers: His denial of God is associated with corruption and wickedness
His belief in God makes him do evil
His search for God makes him turn away
medium.explanation: The fool’s denial of God is followed by the description of corrupt and wicked conduct.
medium.q: What connection does the passage make between the fool’s belief and his actions?

answers: A person who denies God and acts wickedly
medium.explanation: The fool is characterized by denying God in his heart and living corruptly.
medium.q: What does “fool” describe in this passage?

answers: The fool and his corrupt way
medium.explanation: The passage introduces the psalm and describes the fool’s belief and conduct.
medium.q: What is the main subject of the opening passage?

challenge.explanation: The verse specifically says, “The fool hath said in his heart.”
challenge.q: Where does the fool hold this belief?

answers: He becomes corrupt and does abominable iniquity
challenge.explanation: The passage describes the result as corruption and abominable iniquity.
challenge.q: What moral result is associated with the fool’s position?

answers: It is only a prayer from Zion
It provides instruction concerning the fool’s way
challenge.explanation: The word maskil indicates an instructive or contemplative psalm, and the opening teaches about the fool’s way.
challenge.q: What does the psalm’s heading suggest about the passage?

paragraphs.title: The Divine Look from Heaven and the Absence of Good

easy.explanation: The verse says, “God looked down from heaven.”
easy.q: From where did God look upon the children of men?

answers: Someone who understood and sought God
easy.explanation: God looked to see whether there were any who understood and sought Him.
easy.q: What was God looking for among humanity?

easy.explanation: The passage concludes, “There is none that doeth good, no, not one.”
easy.q: What conclusion is given about the people?

answers: The whole generation has turned aside and become filthy
medium.explanation: The passage says that everyone has gone back and become altogether filthy.
medium.q: What does God’s looking down reveal?

answers: Someone who has discernment and seeks God
medium.explanation: The person God seeks is one who understands and searches for Him.
medium.q: What does “understand” mean in this context?

answers: The search reveals that no one does good
The search reveals that Israel is joyful
The search causes the wicked camp to scatter
medium.explanation: God looks for someone who seeks Him, but the conclusion is that no one does good.
medium.q: What is the relationship between God’s search and the conclusion that follows?

answers: God looks and searches, but humanity has turned aside
Humanity rejoices, but God is afraid
Israel is saved, but Jacob is scattered
challenge.explanation: God’s examination is contrasted with the moral failure of humanity.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in the passage?

answers: The complete absence of anyone doing good
The existence of one discerning person
challenge.explanation: The repetition emphasizes the totality of the moral failure: “no, not one.”
challenge.q: What does the repeated statement that there is none doing good emphasize?

answers: God’s looking, His search for a seeker, and the discovery that all have turned aside
Eating bread, scattering bones, and then the heading
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from God’s observation to His search and then to His conclusion about humanity.
challenge.q: What is the order of ideas in the passage?

paragraphs.title: The Wicked Who Harm the People and Do Not Call on God

easy.explanation: The verse refers to “the workers of iniquity.”
easy.q: What are the wicked people called in the verse?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “who eat up my people as they eat bread.”
easy.q: Whom are they described as eating up?

answers: They do not harm the people
They do not call upon God
easy.explanation: The verse ends by saying, “they have not called upon God.”
easy.q: What do the workers of iniquity fail to do?

medium.explanation: The wicked are said to eat up God’s people as they eat bread.
medium.q: What action is compared to eating bread?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes people who practice evil or iniquity.

answers: They harm God’s people and do not call upon Him
They do good and call upon God
They fear and flee from Zion
medium.explanation: Both actions are stated: they consume God’s people and do not call upon God.
medium.q: Which combination describes the wicked in the verse?

answers: The harm is presented as ordinary and without restraint
The wicked are asking for food
The people are not being harmed
challenge.explanation: The comparison emphasizes how routinely and ruthlessly the wicked harm the people.
challenge.q: What does the image of eating bread suggest in this context?

answers: Eating bread versus calling upon God
Harming the people while refusing to call upon God
challenge.explanation: The verse joins their oppression of God’s people with their refusal to call upon Him.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in the verse?

answers: The people are presented as belonging to God
The people are the wicked camp
The people have no connection with God
challenge.explanation: The possessive phrase identifies them as God’s people.
challenge.q: What can be understood from the phrase “my people”?

paragraphs.title: False Fear and the Defeat of the Wicked Camp

easy.explanation: The verse begins, “There were they in great fear.”
easy.q: What did the people experience in the verse?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee.”
easy.q: What did God do to the camp of the enemy?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “thou hast put them to shame.”
easy.q: What did God do to the wicked camp?

answers: God scattered and shamed the enemy
The good people abandoned the nation
medium.explanation: The apparent threat was overturned because God scattered and shamed the enemy.
medium.q: Why was the fear described as fear where no fear was?

answers: The fear was ultimately without a real cause
No one had ever been afraid
medium.explanation: The phrase indicates that the fear proved empty or unfounded.
medium.q: What does “where no fear was” suggest?

answers: He gathered, praised, and drew near
medium.explanation: The verse presents God as scattering the enemy, putting them to shame, and despising them.

answers: Great fear at first, but the enemy is defeated and shamed
Joy at first, followed by prayer
Seeking God at first, followed by doing good
challenge.explanation: The verse moves from great fear to the enemy’s scattering and shame.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the beginning and the end of the verse?

answers: The fear was justified and continued
The fear did not come to pass as expected
No one had ever feared anything
challenge.explanation: The phrase shows that the feared danger did not prevail.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “where no fear was” communicate?

challenge.explanation: To despise them means that God rejected or regarded them with contempt.
challenge.q: What does “despised them” reveal about God’s attitude toward the wicked camp?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion!”
easy.q: From where does the psalm pray that Israel’s salvation will come?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “When God bringeth back the captivity of his people.”
easy.q: What does the psalm ask God to do for His people?

answers: They will be silent and mourn
They will rejoice and be glad
easy.explanation: The verse says, “Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.”
easy.q: How will Jacob and Israel respond?

medium.explanation: The people’s restoration is followed by Jacob’s rejoicing and Israel’s gladness.
medium.q: What is the connection between the restoration of God’s people and their response?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to restoring the people from captivity or distress.
medium.q: What does “bringeth back the captivity” mean in this passage?

answers: Salvation from Zion, restoration of the people, and then joy
medium.explanation: The verse moves from the prayer for salvation to restoration and finally to rejoicing.
medium.q: What is the order of the request and its result?

answers: From the defeat of the wicked to a prayer for Israel’s salvation
From Israel’s prayer to consuming the people
challenge.explanation: After describing God’s rejection of the wicked, the psalm turns to hope for Israel’s salvation.
challenge.q: What is the main transition from the previous verse to this one?

answers: The joy of God’s people under two related names
The difference between the wicked and the righteous
The scattering of the wicked camp
challenge.explanation: The two names refer to God’s people and emphasize their shared joy.
challenge.q: What does the pairing of “Jacob” and “Israel” emphasize?

answers: Hope for salvation, restoration, and rejoicing
An accusation that Israel eats bread
challenge.explanation: The conclusion expresses hope that God will save and restore His people, bringing them joy.
challenge.q: What overall meaning emerges from the psalm’s conclusion?
